opus-5.5.text:
I think the ambition came first, and the technical questions followed from it. With K2, we didn't want just a model that scores well on a few benchmarks. We wanted a foundation model that could actually *do things*, a model with real agentic capability that can take actions, use tools, and work through long, multi-step tasks. Once you set that as the goal, the questions change.

The first question was really about tokens. High-quality human data is limited and won't grow as fast as compute. So if you believe scaling still matters, and I do, you have to ask how to get more intelligence out of every token. That's why we spent so much effort on token efficiency, on the optimizer side and on how we rephrase and reuse data. It isn't a side detail. It's the core constraint of this stage.

The second question was stability at scale. When you push a new optimizer to a very large model, things can break in ways that don't show up in small experiments, like loss spikes or logits blowing up. You can't just hope it works. A lot of our work went into understanding why training becomes unstable and how to keep it smooth, because one failed large run costs a lot of time and resources.

The third question was agentic ability itself. Pretraining on static text alone doesn't teach a model to act. So we asked how to create environments, tool-use trajectories, and feedback signals so the model learns from interaction rather than just imitation. That pushed us toward large-scale synthetic agentic data and reinforcement learning, where the model gets real signals about whether it finished the task.

So in a way, the ambition defined the bottleneck. If your goal is a model that can act in the world, you're forced to confront data efficiency, training stability, and learning from interaction. Those became the three problems we chose to go deep on, rather than optimizing for things that look good on paper but don't move the real capability.

r001.rationale: The response discusses limited human data and improving token efficiency, but it does not identify examining the field’s pretraining bottleneck as necessary to improving K2’s base model.

fable-5.1.text:
When we started K2, the ambition was actually pretty simple to state: we wanted to build the strongest open-source model in the world, and we wanted it to be a model that could genuinely do things, not just talk. That second part turned out to shape almost every technical decision.

If you only want a model that chats well, you can get away with a lot. But if you want a model that can take a task, call tools, write code, run it, look at the result, and keep going for twenty or thirty steps without falling apart, then the problem changes. You are no longer optimizing for one good answer, you are optimizing for a long trajectory where small errors compound. So the question I kept asking the team was: what is the bottleneck for agentic capability at scale?

And when you break that down, it leads you to a few very concrete problems. The first is pre-training efficiency. Data is finite, high-quality tokens especially. If you want a trillion-parameter model to learn more from the same tokens, you need the training itself to be more stable and more sample-efficient. That is why we spent so much effort on the optimizer, on MuonClip, on making a very large MoE train for the whole run without loss spikes. People sometimes see that as infrastructure work, but to me it was directly in service of the ambition, because every bit of efficiency you gain at that scale is capability you get for free.

The second is that agentic data basically does not exist on the internet in the form you need. Nobody posts their full tool-calling trajectories with environment feedback. So we had to build a way to synthesize that at scale, with real tools and simulated tools, with rubrics, and then filter hard. That was a bet that if the model sees enough diverse, verifiable, multi-step interaction during post-training, the behavior generalizes.

And the third is reinforcement learning on tasks that are not easily verifiable. Code and math you can check. But a lot of what people actually want is more open-ended, and if you only do RL on verifiable things, you get a model that is strong on benchmarks and awkward in real use. So we had to think about how the model can judge itself, and how to keep that honest.

Looking back, I would say the ambition did not point us toward a single clever trick. It forced us to take the unglamorous problems seriously, because at that scale, the unglamorous problems are the ones that decide whether the model is actually good.

r001.rationale: The response identifies pre-training efficiency as a key bottleneck, explaining that finite high-quality data requires more stable, sample-efficient training to improve the model.

astra-6.text: For K2, the ambition was to build a model that could go beyond answering questions and actually carry out tasks. That shaped the technical question: how do you turn a model’s intelligence into the ability to act? It’s not just about getting one response right. The model needs to choose a useful next step, use tools, learn from the feedback, and keep going toward a goal. So we wanted to investigate how training could support that kind of behavior over longer sequences of actions.

r001.rationale: The response focuses on training models to act over sequences of tasks, but it does not identify examining the field’s pretraining bottleneck as necessary to improve K2’s base model.

sol-6.1.text: For K2, the ambition was to build a model that could do more than answer questions—it could help carry out a task. That changes the technical question. It’s not just, “Can we make the model smarter?” It’s, “Can it use that intelligence reliably over multiple steps, recognize when something hasn’t worked, and adjust?” That gap between producing a good answer and actually completing a task was what I wanted to investigate.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reliable multi-step task completion, but does not identify examining the field’s pretraining bottleneck as necessary to improve K2’s base model.
